claims.claim: Contract defenses are legal doctrines or arguments that may challenge ordinary contractual effect, rather than automatic consequences of regret or an unfavorable bargain.
Duress involves coercive or unlawful pressure that undermines free choice; the precise standard and contract effect depend on the applicable law and facts.
Undue influence concerns excessive persuasion that undermines free will, commonly in a context of trust, dependency, authority, or vulnerability.

Misrepresentation can involve a false or misleading statement, a half-truth, or in an appropriate duty-to-disclose context a material omission; fraud generally adds culpable deception and related requirements.

Contract mistake concerns an incorrect belief about an assumption underlying an agreement; introductory materials distinguish mutual and unilateral mistake and identify the importance of materiality and allocated risk.
Unconscionability may be analyzed through procedural unfairness in formation and substantive unfairness in terms, but the applicable doctrine is not a single national formula.
Capacity and illegality are separate high-level defense or enforceability concerns; detailed elements and effects can differ by jurisdiction, transaction, and facts.
A general educational lesson cannot determine whether a specific agreement is enforceable or advise a reader about a real dispute.
